verse.text: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
verse.summary: David wrote this psalm for the dedication of his house, looking back on a season when he thought he was finished — sick, low, and sure the pit was next. What he learned is that God's displeasure is brief and His favour lasts a lifetime, and that grief, however real, is a night guest, not a permanent resident. Notice the verse doesn't promise weeping will never come; it promises weeping has a checkout time. If you're in the night right now, don't unpack — morning is already scheduled, and joy is on its way.

sermon.title: He Shall Doubtless Come Again
sermon.excerpt: In a lean year the seed in the farmer's hand was his children's supper, so he walked into the field crying — and planted it anyway. Heaven wrote one word over his harvest that no drought can cancel: doubtless.

bibleStudy.title: Go, and Do Thou Likewise

verses.text: And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead. And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee. Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.

But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.

bibleStudy.excerpt: A lawyer tried to shrink the word "neighbour" down to a size he could manage. Jesus answered with a beaten man on a dangerous road — and let an enemy be the hero.
body: Start with the question underneath the question, because the lawyer in this story was not actually confused. Luke tells you flat out why he opened his mouth — he wanted to "tempt" Jesus, and when that first exchange didn't work, he tried a second one "willing to justify himself." He already knew the answer to eternal life; he recited it back to Jesus perfectly, word for word out of his own Bible: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus even tells him, "Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live." Case closed, you'd think. But a man who has already been told he's right will sometimes keep talking anyway, because what he actually wants isn't an answer — he wants an exit. So he asks the one question every one of us has asked in some version, usually right after we've been caught not loving somebody: "And who is my neighbour?" Translation: how small can I legally make this circle?

Jesus does not hand him a definition. He hands him a dying man on the side of a road, because some questions only a story can actually answer. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead." That road was no polite metaphor — it was a seventeen-mile drop through bare limestone and blind switchbacks, famous in that world for exactly this, robbers working it like a trade. Jesus's first listeners didn't hear "once upon a time." They heard a headline. A man beaten, stripped, and left to die in the sun, breathing but not for much longer, on a road everybody in that crowd had either traveled or avoided for this exact reason.

Here comes help. Twice. "And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side." Read that twice, because Luke wants you to feel the repetition land like a second gut-punch in the same spot as the first. Not one failure of mercy — two, back to back, and not from strangers to holiness but from its own staff. The priest ran the temple. The Levite assisted him in it. These were the two men in the entire story most professionally qualified to define mercy, and both of them looked at a dying man and did math instead — time, ceremonial defilement, the cost of being late, whatever the excuse was that morning — and the math came out in favor of the other side of the road. Funny how often religion can walk right past the exact person it was built to serve, as long as it's wearing the right robe while it does it.

And then the twist nobody in that crowd wanted. "But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him." A Samaritan. To a first-century Jewish audience, that word didn't mean neighbor, it meant enemy — a people they wouldn't worship with, wouldn't eat with, wouldn't even walk through the same town as if they could help it. Jesus could have made the hero a layman, an off-duty soldier, anybody acceptable. He picked the one man in the parable this crowd had already written off as incapable of mercy, and made him the only one who had any. Let that sit on you for a second, because it still lands the same way today: the person you've decided is too far outside your theology, your politics, your respectable circle to teach you anything about God — that might be exactly who God is using to show you what you've been missing.

Now watch what mercy actually costs when it stops being a feeling and starts being a verb, because this is the part we skip past to get to the moral. "And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee." Count what he spent: his oil, his wine, his own transportation — he put the dying man on the animal and walked — his time, his cash, and an open-ended promise to cover whatever the bill came to after he was long gone. He didn't glance, sigh, and keep moving with a prayer for the guy. He stopped, poured his own resources into a stranger's wound, and left a blank check behind him on a road where he himself was still the suspicious outsider. That's the whole difference between feeling sorry for somebody and actually being their neighbor.

So Jesus flips the lawyer's question back at him, and the flip is the whole sermon. "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among thieves?" Notice what Jesus did there — the lawyer asked who qualifies as my neighbor, a noun, a category, a fence he could build and then stand safely inside of. Jesus answers with a verb. He never tells him who counts. He asks who acted like one. You cannot locate your neighbor by drawing the right boundary around your compassion; you can only become one by crossing a boundary with it. The lawyer wanted a smaller list of people he owed love to. Jesus handed him back a bigger definition of what love actually does.

And none of this was new material, which is the part that should really humble you. Centuries before this road, before this priest, before this Samaritan, the law the lawyer had already memorized said it plainly: "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Jesus isn't introducing a doctrine that morning. He's holding up a mirror to a command this man had been reciting his whole life and never once applied to a bleeding stranger on a dangerous road. That's usually how conviction actually works on us too — not new information, just an old verse finally catching up to an old excuse.

And in case anybody wants to keep this safely filed away as a nice story about a nice Samaritan, the apostle John comes along later and nails the application down in plain economic terms, no parable required: "But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." In word, neither in tongue. John is not impressed by your prayer for someone you watched suffer and did nothing about. He asks the Samaritan's question in letter form: you had the oil and the wine and the beast and the two pence — did you stop, or did you just feel bad while you kept walking?

Here's my real question for you today, and I want you to actually name the road and the person, not just nod at the general principle: who have you already built a theological, cultural, or just plain convenient excuse to pass by on the other side of? Maybe it's a family member who embarrasses you. Maybe it's the coworker whose politics make your skin crawl. Maybe it's the stranger at the light with the sign, and you've got six good reasons memorized for why that one's not your problem. The priest and the Levite had good reasons too. Scripture didn't bother recording a single one of them, because on that road, reasons for not stopping don't make it into the Book of Life — only the stopping does.

So here's how the story actually ends, and it's not a moral, it's a command: "Go, and do thou likewise." Not go and feel something. Not go and agree in principle. Go — and do. Pour your own oil on somebody else's wound this week. Spend your own two pence on somebody who can't repay you and never will. Love in deed and in truth, not in word, neither in tongue, because the whole Book has already told you what you are when you don't — and it's not an unfortunate theological technicality, it's a mirror with your name already in it. Stop walking past the bleeding man looking for a cleaner definition of neighbor. Become one. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that my tears are not wasted — they are seed!
I will not eat my seed because I am hungry!
I go forth bearing precious seed, and I shall doubtless come again with rejoicing!
Every tear I have cried in Your will is in Your bottle and in Your book!
What I buried in obedience is not lost — it is working!
Turn again my captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south!
Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning!
I will not be weary in well doing — in due season I shall reap, for I will not faint!
I went out with a handful; I am coming back with sheaves!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. They that sow in tears shall reap in joy! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: No Table Holds My Name
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not about any one dream scene — it meets every evil altar, every midnight summons, every witchcraft table set to feed, mark, or bind you while you sleep. Whatever shape the invitation takes, you were never built to answer it. Pray this aloud before you close your eyes, in Jesus' name.
points: Father, Your Word declares in Deuteronomy 18:11, "Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer" — every necromancer, every familiar spirit, every evil summons sent to fetch me into a witchcraft gathering tonight is forbidden ground; it has no legal access to my spirit, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the record of 1 Samuel 28:7, where Saul said, "Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her" — I decree that no agent of darkness shall seek me out, enquire after me, or summon my spirit to any altar, séance, or coven tonight; I am sought only by my Good Shepherd, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, as in Judges 6:28, "...the altar of Baal was cast down, and the grove was cut down that was by it..." — every altar raised against my life in the dream realm tonight, every shrine built to hold my name, is cast down and cut down before the sun rises, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I stand on Isaiah 65:11, where it is written against those that "prepare a table for that troop, and...furnish the drink offering unto that number" — every table spread for me by witchcraft tonight, every seat reserved for me at a gathering I never agreed to, is overturned, and I refuse the portion poured out there, in Jesus' mighty name!

By the word of Malachi 1:7, "Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar..." — every polluted bread, every defiled meal, every strange food set before me in a dream tonight is rejected; I will not eat what darkness has prepared, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Your Word declares in Psalm 69:22, "Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap" — I decree that every table set to trap me tonight becomes a snare to the hand that set it; let the trap close on the trapper, not on me, in Jesus' mighty name!

I take my stand with Daniel 1:8, "Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank" — I purpose in my heart tonight that I will not defile myself with any portion served to me by a strange hand in my sleep, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the authority of 1 Corinthians 10:21, "Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils" — I renounce every fellowship, every covenant meal, every cup offered me at any table of devils tonight; I am a partaker of the Lord's table alone, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, according to Esther 7:10, "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai" — every gallows, every trap, every altar prepared for my downfall tonight swallows up the one who prepared it; let every plotter fall into their own plot, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I decree by Psalm 35:8, "Let destruction come upon him at unawares; and let his net that he hath hid catch himself: into that very destruction let him fall" — every net hidden for me in the dream realm tonight catches the hand that hid it, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, Your Word declares in Psalm 23:5, "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over" — the only table set for me tonight is the one You prepare; my head is anointed, my cup overflows, and no enemy's table can compete, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the promise of Luke 22:30, "That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom..." — I decree I belong at the King's table and no other; every evil invitation is declined, for my place is already set in the kingdom, in Jesus' mighty name!

So I seal tonight with Revelation 19:9, "Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb" — this is the only supper my name is written for. Every other altar, table, and summons is null and void over my life. I will wake in the morning untouched, unmarked, and unbound, seated only at the table of my King, in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
